title: People with severe paralysis regained control of a computer at home
summary: A Synchron Stentrode implant with a participant-specific decoder turned attempted movements into clicks, and with eye tracking it let two people with ALS use a computer at home.
account: Two people with ALS received a Stentrode implant at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. Attempted movements generated computer clicks, while an eye tracker moved the cursor. Participant 1 used a support-vector machine, and participant 2 used a manually tuned threshold classifier. They began use at home without research staff on days 86 and 71 after implantation, although a caregiver still helped set up the system. Both could text, shop, and check finances. In a typing task, the two participants typed 13.81 and 20.10 correct characters per minute. A later report followed four implanted participants, including the original two, for 12 months. It reported no serious device-related events and eight mild device effects. In a systematic review published on 10 May 2025, researchers led from the Mayo Clinic, who list no tie to Synchron, report that two clinical studies showed six people with ALS using an endovascular brain-computer interface for digital communication. They judge that the early results are promising and that clinical data remain scarce.
purpose: Restore digital device control for people with severe paralysis without open-brain surgery
system: Synchron Stentrode with a participant-specific decoder and Tobii Dynavox eye tracking
developer: Synchron Inc. with the University of Melbourne
deployer: Royal Melbourne Hospital (implantation and follow-up); participants' homes (use)
segment: People with ALS and severe upper-limb paralysis

ratings.reason: Participants regained sustained control of everyday computer tasks at home. No separate societal outcome was measured.

ai_role.statement: Participant 1 used a support-vector machine trained on movement attempts. Participant 2 used a manually tuned threshold classifier. Both converted brain signals into clicks, while an eye tracker handled cursor movement. The measured benefit belonged to the combined system.

evidence.citation: Oxley TJ, Yoo PE, Rind GS, et al. (2021). Motor neuroprosthesis implanted with neurointerventional surgery improves capacity for activities of daily living tasks in severe paralysis: first in-human experience. Journal of NeuroInterventional Surgery 13(2):102-108.
evidence.title: Motor neuroprosthesis implanted with neurointerventional surgery improves capacity for activities of daily living tasks in severe paralysis: first in-human experience
evidence.quote: Completion of IADL tasks including text messaging, online shopping and managing finances independently was demonstrated in both participants.

evidence.citation: Peter Mitchell et al., “Assessment of Safety of a Fully Implanted Endovascular Brain-Computer Interface for Severe Paralysis in 4 Patients: The Stentrode With Thought-Controlled Digital Switch (SWITCH) Study,” JAMA Neurology 80, no. 3 (2023): 270–278, doi:10.1001/jamaneurol.2022.4847. Published online January 9, 2023.
evidence.title: Assessment of Safety of a Fully Implanted Endovascular Brain-Computer Interface for Severe Paralysis in 4 Patients: The Stentrode With Thought-Controlled Digital Switch (SWITCH) Study

evidence.citation: Ognard J, El Hajj G, Verma O, Ghozy S, Kadirvel R, Kallmes DF, Brinjikji W, Advances in endovascular brain computer interface: Systematic review and future implications, Journal of Neuroscience Methods 420:110471, published online 10 May 2025. The authors work at the Mayo Clinic, Brest University Hospital and PGIMER Chandigarh, and their disclosures list no tie to Synchron. In their PRISMA review they cite both Stentrode clinical papers, report that two clinical studies showed six people with ALS using an endovascular BCI for digital communication and judge that clinical data remain scarce.
evidence.title: Advances in endovascular brain computer interface: Systematic review and future implications
evidence.quote: Two clinical studies reported six ALS patients successfully using an endovascular BCI for digital communication.
